The cells that read the Fukushima data are marked `#| fukudata`. The
outputs on this page come from a local run.

A data-centric approach trains a model on the data at hand, studies its
errors, and collects more samples where it fails. It rests on a
hypothesis: a model, a deep-learning model in particular, makes its
largest errors on samples unlike those it trained on. If so, the samples
to collect can be chosen from the spectra, before any wet chemistry.

This notebook tests the hypothesis on the Cs-137 ratio and `log1p(Kex)`,
with the folds grouped by field of `20_grouped_cv` and
`23_field_baselines`, so that every test field is new to the model. It
compares the absolute out-of-fold error with three signals available
before measuring: how far a sample lies from the training samples, how
much bootstrap models disagree on it, and how extreme its prediction is.
It then looks at where the errors are instead, and whether the error of
each field follows its location, soil type or land use.

## Data and models

As in `23_field_baselines`: the spectra after SNV and the first
derivative, and block 4 of the OSSL Kex and CEC models. The spectra are
also used with the direction of the IAEA artefact of `21_iaea` projected
out, because the artefact changes between measurement sessions and could
make a sample look unusual for reasons unrelated to the soil:

``` python
fuku = load_fuku()
ids = fuku.sample_ids
src = fuku.source.reindex(ids)
ratio = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(fuku_path()/'reference'/f'cs137_ratio_{s}.csv', usecols=['ID', 'exCs137_totalCs137']) for s in ('train', 'test')])
ratio = ratio.assign(ID=ratio.ID.astype(str)).set_index('ID')['exCs137_totalCs137']
targets = {'Cs-137 ratio': ratio.reindex(ids).to_numpy(), 'Kex': np.log1p(src['soil_ex_K2O'].to_numpy(dtype=float) / mg_k2o_per_cmolc)}
fields = src['field_no'].astype(str).to_numpy()
coords = src[['Field_place(latitude)', 'Field_place(longitude)']].apply(pd.to_numeric, errors='coerce').to_numpy()
soil, land = src['Soil_type_describe'].fillna('unknown').astype(str).to_numpy(), src['fieldtype'].fillna('unknown').astype(str).to_numpy()
pipe = preprocessings()['snv_d1']
Xd = pipe.fit_transform(fuku.spectra)
B4 = np.hstack([layer_features(load_pretrained(n), Xd)['block 4'] for n in ('ossl_kex_snv_d1', 'ossl_cec_snv_d1')])
pw = shared_wns[:-1]
snv = lambda A: (A - A.mean(1, keepdims=True)) / A.std(1, keepdims=True)
pids = [i for i in sorted(set(bruker_files()) & set(spa_files()), key=int) if i not in excluded]
p_tb = (snv(load_fuku(pw, pids).spectra) - snv(load_bruker(pw, pids).spectra)).mean(0)
v = pipe.named_steps['deriv'].transform(np.r_[p_tb, p_tb[-1]][None])[0]
spaces = {'spectra': Xd, 'spectra, artefact removed': epo_project(Xd, (v / np.linalg.norm(v))[:, None]), 'block 4': B4}
ridge = (make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge()), {'ridge__alpha': np.logspace(-1, 6, 15)})
Xd.shape, B4.shape
```

## Novelty and uncertainty

`novelty` is the mean distance from each test sample to its `k` nearest
training samples, on whitened PCA scores fitted to the training samples,
where the Euclidean distance is the Mahalanobis distance:

``` python
def novelty(
    Xtr, # Training features, one row per sample
    Xte, # Test features
    k=10, # Number of neighbours
    n=20, # Number of PCA components
)->np.ndarray: # One distance per test sample
    "Mean Mahalanobis distance from each row of `Xte` to its `k` nearest rows of `Xtr`, on `n` whitened PCA components of `Xtr`"
    p = PCA(n, whiten=True, random_state=0).fit(Xtr)
    return NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(p.transform(Xtr)).kneighbors(p.transform(Xte))[0].mean(1)
```

``` python
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xtr_ = rng.normal(size=(200, 5))
nv_ = novelty(Xtr_, np.r_[np.zeros((1, 5)), np.full((1, 5), 4.)], n=5)
assert nv_[1] > 3 * nv_[0]
```

Ridge on the spectra and on block 4, with its penalty chosen by inner
folds, gives the out-of-fold predictions. In each fold, the novelty of
each test sample in the three feature spaces, and the uncertainty: the
standard deviation of the predictions of 10 ridge models, each fitted
with the chosen penalty on a bootstrap resample of the training fields:

``` python
oof, err, nov, unc = {}, {}, {}, {}
for t, y_all in targets.items():
    ok = np.isfinite(y_all)
    y, fo = y_all[ok], fields[ok]
    folds = group_folds(fo)
    for m, X in [('spectra', Xd[ok]), ('block 4', B4[ok])]:
        p, chosen = oof_preds(*ridge, X, y, folds, fo)
        oof[t, m], err[t, m] = p, np.abs(y - p)
        nov[t, m] = {k: np.full(len(y), np.nan) for k in spaces}
        unc[t, m] = np.full(len(y), np.nan)
        for j, f in enumerate(np.unique(folds)):
            tr, te = folds != f, folds == f
            for k, S in spaces.items(): nov[t, m][k][te] = novelty(S[ok][tr], S[ok][te])
            rng, uf, bp = np.random.default_rng(j), np.unique(fo[tr]), []
            for b in range(10):
                sel = tr & np.isin(fo, rng.choice(uf, len(uf), replace=True))
                bp.append(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=chosen[j]['ridge__alpha'])).fit(X[sel], y[sel]).predict(X[te]))
            unc[t, m][te] = np.std(bp, axis=0)
```

The Spearman correlation of the absolute error with each signal, and the
RMSE of the fifth of the samples with the highest signal over that of
the fifth with the lowest. The predicted extreme is the distance of the
prediction from the mean prediction:

``` python
def fifth_ratio(e, s):
    q = pd.qcut(s, 5, labels=False)
    return np.sqrt((e[q == 4]**2).mean() / (e[q == 0]**2).mean())
rows = {}
for (t, m), e in err.items():
    sig = {f'novelty, {k}': s for k, s in nov[t, m].items()} | {'uncertainty': unc[t, m], 'predicted extreme': np.abs(oof[t, m] - oof[t, m].mean())}
    for k, s in sig.items(): rows[t, m, k] = {'ρ': stats.spearmanr(e, s)[0], 'RMSE ratio, top / bottom fifth': fifth_ratio(e, s)}
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.unstack(1).round(3)
```

## Where the errors are

For ridge on block 4: the share of the residual variance between fields
(`field_variance` of `23_field_baselines`, across years), the slope of
the residual on the measured value, the Spearman correlation of the
absolute error with the distance of the measured value from its mean,
and the standard deviation of the predictions over that of the measured
values:

``` python
rows = {}
for t, y_all in targets.items():
    ok = np.isfinite(y_all)
    y, r = y_all[ok], y_all[ok] - oof[t, 'block 4']
    rows[t] = {'residual share between fields': field_variance(r, fields[ok])['share between'], 'slope of residual on measured value': np.polyfit(y, r, 1)[0],
               'ρ, |error| and |measured − mean|': stats.spearmanr(np.abs(r), np.abs(y - y.mean()))[0], 'sd of predictions / sd of measured': oof[t, 'block 4'].std() / y.std()}
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)
```

## Field residuals

The mean residual of each field, from ridge on block 4, with the field’s
coordinates, soil type and land use:

``` python
fres = {}
for t, y_all in targets.items():
    ok = np.isfinite(y_all)
    d = pd.DataFrame({'field': fields[ok], 'r': y_all[ok] - oof[t, 'block 4'], 'lat': coords[ok, 0], 'lon': coords[ok, 1], 'soil': soil[ok], 'land': land[ok]})
    fres[t] = d.groupby('field').agg(r=('r', 'mean'), lat=('lat', 'mean'), lon=('lon', 'mean'), soil=('soil', 'first'), land=('land', 'first'))
{t: len(f) for t, f in fres.items()}
```

    {'Cs-137 ratio': 391, 'Kex': 391}

`morans_i` measures how much the residuals of nearby fields agree, with
weights that average the `k` nearest fields, and tests it against random
permutations of the residuals over the fields:

``` python
def morans_i(
    v, # One value per location
    xy, # Coordinates of each location
    k=5, # Number of neighbours
    n_perm=999, # Number of permutations
    seed=0, # Seed for the permutations
)->tuple: # Moran's I, and its one-sided permutation p-value
    "Moran's I of `v` with row-standardised weights on the `k` nearest neighbours by `xy`"
    ix = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k + 1).fit(xy).kneighbors(xy)[1][:, 1:]
    I = lambda z: (z * z[ix].mean(1)).sum() / (z**2).sum()
    z, rng = v - v.mean(), np.random.default_rng(seed)
    i0 = I(z)
    return i0, (1 + sum(I(rng.permutation(z)) >= i0 for _ in range(n_perm))) / (n_perm + 1)
```

``` python
xy_ = np.c_[np.arange(100.), np.zeros(100)]
i_, p_ = morans_i(np.sin(np.arange(100) / 10), xy_, n_perm=199)
assert i_ > 0.8 and p_ < 0.01
i_, p_ = morans_i(np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=100), xy_, n_perm=199)
assert abs(i_) < 0.2
```

Moran’s I on the five nearest fields, the correlation of each field’s
residual with the mean residual of its nearest 1 to 20 fields, and the
median distance to the nearest field in degrees:

``` python
rows = {}
for t, f in fres.items():
    xy, r = f[['lat', 'lon']].to_numpy(), f.r.to_numpy()
    i, p = morans_i(r, xy)
    rows[t] = {"Moran's I": i, 'p': p}
    for k in [1, 5, 10, 20]:
        ix = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k + 1).fit(xy).kneighbors(xy)[1][:, 1:]
        rows[t][f'r, mean of {k} nearest'] = np.corrcoef(r, r[ix].mean(1))[0, 1]
    rows[t]['median distance to the nearest field'] = np.median(NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=2).fit(xy).kneighbors(xy)[0][:, 1])
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4)
```

The share of the variance of the field residuals that soil type, land
use and their combination explain (η²), with a Kruskal-Wallis test over
the groups of at least 5 fields:

``` python
def eta2(r, g): return ((pd.Series(r).groupby(g).transform('mean') - r.mean())**2).sum() / ((r - r.mean())**2).sum()
rows = {}
for t, f in fres.items():
    for k, g in [('soil type', f.soil), ('land use', f.land), ('soil type × land use', f.soil + ', ' + f.land)]:
        g = g.to_numpy()
        rows[t, k] = {'η²': eta2(f.r.to_numpy(), g), 'p': stats.kruskal(*[f.r.to_numpy()[g == u] for u in np.unique(g) if (g == u).sum() >= 5]).pvalue}
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(4)
```

## Findings

The errors are not where the model has seen few similar samples. For the
Cs-137 ratio, the absolute error barely correlates with novelty in any
feature space (Spearman −0.03 to 0.05), with the disagreement of
bootstrap models (0.04 and 0.09) or with how extreme the prediction is
(−0.08 and −0.05). The fifth of the samples that each signal ranks
highest has an RMSE 1.01 to 1.18 times that of the lowest fifth. For Kex
the signals do slightly better: Spearman 0.03 to 0.13, and RMSE ratios
of 1.22 to 1.52, highest for novelty in block 4. Removing the direction
of the IAEA artefact does not change novelty’s relation with the error,
so measurement sessions do not hide one.

The errors are field offsets and a pull towards the mean. Between 53%
(Cs-137 ratio) and 59% (Kex) of the residual variance lies between
fields, so the model is wrong by a similar amount on every sample of a
field. The predictions are compressed: their standard deviation is 78%
and 58% of that of the measured values, the residual rises with the
measured value (slopes 0.41 and 0.70), and the error grows with distance
from the mean (Spearman 0.26 and 0.54). The fields with high or low
values do not look unusual in their spectra.

The field offsets follow location a little. Moran’s I of the field
residuals on the five nearest fields is 0.13 for the Cs-137 ratio and
0.09 for Kex (p 0.001 and 0.002). A field’s residual correlates with the
mean residual of its nearest 1 to 20 fields at 0.20 to 0.24 for the
ratio and 0.17 to 0.23 for Kex. The nearest field lies a median of
0.0075°, about 0.8 km, away.

Soil type and land use explain nothing for the Cs-137 ratio: η² is 1% to
4%, with p 0.10 to 0.63. For Kex, land use explains 13% (p \< 0.001),
and soil type with land use 18%. The model under-predicts upland fields
(+0.03 to +0.09 on `log1p`) and over-predicts paddy fields (−0.03 to
−0.15), within every soil type. Adding land use to the model’s inputs
takes up most of this (`23_field_baselines`).

For sampling guided by the model, these data give little to steer by.
The spectra and the model do not flag the samples they will get wrong.
Location helps a little for both properties, and land use for Kex. Over
80% of the variance of the field offsets is explained by none of these.
What drives it is not in these data. Field management, such as potassium
fertilisation, deep ploughing, topsoil removal and the history of
remediation since 2011, is the obvious candidate to obtain.

All models here are ridge regressions, on the spectra or on frozen block
4. The uncertainty of an ensemble of CNNs was not tested.
